211.title: The light in the sun (15.7–15.15)
211.hook: Krishna says the brightness of the sun, the moon and the fire is his
211.tomorrow: The two and the one beyond (15.16–15.20)
211.howItsDone: Some Hindu families and communities recite Gita chapter fifteen before meals; verse 15.14 describes the divine as the fire of digestion, which makes it a natural mealtime reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday: ashvattha, the tree with roots above. The whole world of change as an upside-down fig, cut with the axe of not clinging. Your line was upside-down tree. Did you loosen one finger? Day two hundred eleven.

The power goes out at night. The fridge goes quiet, the screen goes black. Someone finds a candle and strikes a match, and a small flame fills the room. Outside, the moon is lighting the street. And the whole time, without anyone noticing, a body keeps its own quiet warmth, turning the day's food into heat. Light in the sky, light in the flame, warmth inside a person: a chain of light and heat. Chapter fifteen walks down that exact chain, link by link, and at every link Krishna says the same thing: that's me.
screen: `A CANDLE IN THE DARK.` → `THE MOON OVER THE STREET.` → `WARMTH INSIDE A PERSON.`

segments.voice: It starts with you. Verse seven: a fragment of me, eternal, became the living being in the world of life. Mamaivamsha: a part of my own self. It draws the senses and the mind to itself. Verse eight gives a gentle picture: when that living self takes a body and leaves it, it carries the senses along, the way the wind carries scent from a flower. You can't see it go, but something has moved. Verse ten: the confused don't see it, staying or leaving. Those with the eye of wisdom do. Then the chain of light. Verse twelve: the brightness in the sun that lights the whole world, and the light in the moon, and the light in fire: know that light as mine. Verse thirteen: entering the earth, I hold up all beings with my energy. Becoming the juicy moon, soma, I nourish the plants. Verse fourteen: becoming the fire of digestion in living bodies, joined with the breath going in and out, I digest the four kinds of food. So in this chapter, the divine isn't only far off. Krishna says he is the warmth in the belly after dinner. And verse fifteen brings it all the way home. I am seated in the heart of all. From me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. I am what all the Vedas are trying to know. Your line today is in Krishna's voice. When the Gita says I am the light, it's Krishna speaking, and the chapter traces that light everywhere, from the sun to the heart. That's the word today: the light in the sun.
screen: `A FRAGMENT OF ME, IN YOU.` · `LIGHT IN SUN, MOON AND FIRE.` · `THE FIRE THAT DIGESTS YOUR FOOD.` · `SEATED IN THE HEART OF ALL.` · then, large: `THE LIGHT IN THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Sit, and trace the chain in your own body. Feel any warmth: your hands, your chest, your belly. That warmth started as sunlight. Follow it back: from your belly to the meal, from the meal to the field, from the field to the sun. Then turn around and follow it home again, to the center of your chest. Rest there, where verse fifteen says the light is seated. The bell holds the time.
Tejas, brilliance, radiance. Gita fifteen, twelve: the brightness in the sun, the moon and the fire is Krishna's light; verse fifteen says that light is seated in every heart.
Your line: I am the light. Krishna's words. Today, before you eat, pause for one breath and think of the chain: sun, field, fire, you. Day two hundred eleven.

212.title: The two and the one beyond (15.16–15.20)
212.hook: the perishable, the imperishable, and the highest person beyond both
212.howItsDone: Purushottama, the highest person, is a name of Krishna and Vishnu; some Hindus memorize Gita chapter fifteen, which names Purushottama near its close, and recite it whole.

segments.voice: Yesterday: tejas, the light in the sun. Sun, moon, fire, the fire in your belly, and the light seated in every heart. Your line, in Krishna's voice, was I am the light. Today, the chapter's last and shortest teaching. Day two hundred twelve.

Look at a wave. It rises, curls, crashes, and it's gone. Now look at the ocean under it. The ocean doesn't crash. It was there before this wave, and it'll be there after. So there are two things: the wave that passes and the water that stays. Chapter fifteen doesn't stop there. In five short verses, it says there are two, and then there's a third, beyond both. And it ends the chapter with a claim: know this, and you've done what you came to do.
screen: `THE WAVE THAT PASSES.` → `THE WATER THAT STAYS.` → `AND ONE BEYOND BOTH.`

segments.voice: Verse sixteen. There are two persons in this world, the perishable and the imperishable. Kshara, the perishable, is all beings: every body, every life that begins and ends. Akshara, the imperishable, is called kutastha, the one that stands firm, unchanging. Verse seventeen: but the highest person is another, called the supreme self, the undying Lord who enters the three worlds and holds them up. Verse eighteen: because I am beyond the perishable, and higher even than the imperishable, I am known in the world and in the Veda as Purushottama. The highest person. Purushottama is still a name for Krishna and for Vishnu. Here, the schools read carefully and differently. For Ramanuja and his school, the three are real and distinct: changing beings, unchanging souls, and the Lord beyond and within both. For Advaita teachers, the highest person is the one reality, and the other two are how it appears to us. Then verse nineteen: whoever, free of confusion, knows me as the highest person, knows everything, and worships me with their whole being. And verse twenty ends the chapter: this is the most secret teaching, Arjuna. Knowing this, a person becomes wise, and has done all there is to do. Just five verses, and the chapter calls itself the most secret teaching. That's why its last word to you is short: know this. That's the word today: the two and the one beyond.

segments.voice: Sit, and notice what's changing. The breath, in and out. Sounds arriving and leaving. Thoughts passing. That's the perishable. Now notice what hasn't changed since you sat down: the plain fact of being aware. That's closer to the unchanging. Then, without trying to picture anything, rest your attention on whatever holds both. You don't have to name it. Just let the sitting be wide enough to include it. The bell holds the time.
Purushottama, the highest person. Gita fifteen: the perishable and the imperishable, and beyond both, Purushottama, higher even than the imperishable.
Your line: know this. Today, when something ends, a meeting, a song, a day, notice for one breath that something in you watched it end and didn't. Day two hundred twelve.

213.title: The divine qualities (16.1–16.5)
213.hook: chapter sixteen lists twenty-six qualities, and the first one is fearlessness
213.howItsDone: Some Hindu teachers use Gita 16.1–16.3 as a list of virtues to cultivate; the opening pair, abhaya (fearlessness) and sattva-samshuddhi (purity of heart), is sometimes singled out.

segments.voice: Yesterday: purushottama, the two and the one beyond. The perishable, the imperishable, and the highest person beyond both. Your line was know this. Did you notice something in you watch a day end? Day two hundred thirteen.

If you had to write down the qualities of a good person, what would come first? Kindness, maybe. Honesty. Generosity. Courage might not make the top of the list. Chapter sixteen of the Gita puts it at the top. It opens with a long list, the qualities of someone born, as it says, to a divine inheritance. And the very first word, before truth, before compassion, before anything, is abhaya. Fearlessness. It's worth asking why.
screen: `WHAT COMES FIRST IN A GOOD PERSON?` → `KINDNESS? HONESTY?` → `THE GITA SAYS: FEARLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Verses one to three are one long sentence. Fearlessness. Purity of heart. Steadiness in knowledge and practice. Giving. Self-control. Sacrifice. Study of scripture. Discipline. Straightness. Then: doing no harm, truth, freedom from anger, letting go, peace, not gossiping about others, kindness to all beings, not being greedy, gentleness, modesty, not being fickle. And to close: energy, forgiveness, endurance, cleanliness, no malice, no excess pride. Counted one by one, the list comes to twenty-six. Krishna calls them daivi sampad, the divine inheritance, like a fortune you're born into. Why fearlessness first? The text doesn't say. One answer teachers give: without it, the others don't hold. It's hard to tell the truth if you're afraid. Hard to forgive, hard to give, hard to stay gentle. Fear quietly bends everything else. And the second word, sattva-samshuddhi, purity of heart, is about what's underneath: clean motives, not only clean hands. Together they make today's line. Verse four gives the opposite list, briefly: hypocrisy, arrogance, too much pride, anger, harshness and ignorance. Tomorrow we'll look at that side. Verse five: the divine inheritance leads to freedom, the other to bondage. And then Krishna turns to Arjuna, who began this whole conversation overcome with grief, and says something gentle: do not grieve, Arjuna. You were born to the divine inheritance. It isn't a list to feel bad about. Krishna tells Arjuna the inheritance is already his. That's the word today: the divine qualities.
screen: `TWENTY-SIX QUALITIES.` · `FEARLESSNESS FIRST.` · `PURITY OF HEART UNDERNEATH.` · `DON'T GRIEVE. IT'S ALREADY HIS.` · then, large: `THE DIVINE QUALITIES.`

segments.voice: Sit, and find one small fear you're carrying today. A conversation you're avoiding. An email you haven't sent. Don't solve it. Just look at it. Breathe in, and feel where the fear sits in your body. Breathe out, and let that place soften a little. Then ask quietly: if this fear were a little smaller, what would I do? Let the answer come, or not. The bell holds the time.
Abhaya, fearlessness, no fear. Gita sixteen, one to five: the first of twenty-six qualities of the divine inheritance, daivi sampad, alongside purity of heart.
Your line: fearlessness, purity. Today, do one thing you've been avoiding because of a small fear, and do it with a clean motive. Day two hundred thirteen.

214.title: The demonic (16.6–16.20)
214.hook: the Gita's portrait of the other inheritance sounds uncomfortably modern
214.howItsDone: Hindu teachers often read Gita 16 as a mirror for self-examination rather than a way to label others; the three gates of 16.21, kama, krodha and lobha (desire, anger, greed), are widely quoted.

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhaya, the divine qualities. Twenty-six of them, starting with fearlessness and purity of heart. Your line was fearlessness, purity. Did you do the thing you'd been avoiding? Today, the other list. Day two hundred fourteen.

Hear the word demonic and you probably picture horns, fire, a horror movie. The Gita's picture is much quieter, and more unsettling. It's a person lying awake at night, running the numbers. I got this today. Tomorrow I'll get that. This is mine, and that will be mine too. I beat that rival, and I'll beat the others. Who is like me? It sounds less like a monster and more like a very busy, very anxious person. Maybe someone we've all been, for an evening or two.
screen: `NOT HORNS AND FIRE.` → `SOMEONE AWAKE, RUNNING THE NUMBERS.` → `WHO IS LIKE ME?`

segments.voice: Verse six: there are two kinds of beings in this world, the divine and the asuric, usually translated demonic. In Hindu stories the asuras are the gods' rivals, powerful and proud. Here the word describes a way of living. Verses seven and eight: such people don't know when to act and when to hold back. They say the world has no truth, no ground, no God, and runs on desire alone. Verse ten: gripped by desire that can never be filled, full of hypocrisy, pride and arrogance. Then verses twelve to fifteen, the monologue from the hook. Bound by hundreds of hopes, they pile up wealth by any means. This I gained today, this wish I'll fulfill. I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, strong and happy. Who else is like me? Even their rituals and their giving, verse seventeen says, are done for show, sacrifice in name only. The Gita's verdict is severe: this road leads downward, again and again. Many teachers, especially modern ones, read this chapter less as a label for other people and more as a mirror, though some classical commentators read it as a portrait of a kind of soul. Every one of us has an evening when the monologue runs. And then verse twenty-one names where it all starts, three gates to hell that destroy the self: kama, desire; krodha, anger; and lobha, greed. Shut those three, the Gita says, and a person begins to walk toward the highest. Notice: the gates aren't beliefs or groups of people. They're three movements inside anyone. That's the word today: the demonic.
screen: `TWO KINDS OF BEINGS.` · `THIS IS MINE. WHO IS LIKE ME?` · `A MIRROR, NOT A LABEL.` · `DESIRE, ANGER, GREED.` · then, large: `THE DEMONIC.`

segments.voice: Sit, and listen for the monologue. Is there a list running? Something to get, someone to beat, something that's mine? Don't argue with it. Just hear it, the way you'd hear a radio in another room. Then check the three gates. Is desire pulling? Is anger simmering? Is there a grasping for more? Wherever one is open, breathe out slowly, and let it close a little. The bell holds the time.
The demonic. Gita sixteen: the asuric way of living, restless, proud and grasping, and the three gates that lead there: desire, anger and greed.
Your line: the three gates of hell. Desire, anger, greed. Today, when you feel one of them swing open, name it, and take one breath before you walk through. Day two hundred fourteen.

215.title: Follow the scripture, not desire (16.21–16.24)
215.hook: chapter sixteen ends by asking what you steer by
215.howItsDone: Some Hindus look to shastra, the Vedas and the texts that follow them as taught by a guru or family tradition, for guidance on ritual and conduct; Gita 16.24 is quoted for scripture as the measure of right action.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the demonic, and the monologue of this is mine, who is like me. Your line was the three gates of hell: desire, anger, greed. Did you catch one swinging open? Today, what to steer by instead. Day two hundred fifteen.

A small boat at night. No stars, no map, no compass. The only thing the sailor has is the wind, and the wind keeps changing. The boat goes wherever it's pushed, and calls it a journey. Now hand the sailor a chart that people before them drew, marking the rocks. They can still choose their course. But now they know where the rocks are. Chapter sixteen closes with that choice: steer by the wind of whatever you want right now, or by a chart.
screen: `A BOAT AT NIGHT, NO STARS.` → `ONLY THE WIND.` → `OR A CHART OF THE ROCKS.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-two picks up yesterday's three gates. Whoever is free of those three doors of darkness does what is good for their own self, and goes to the highest. Then verse twenty-three: whoever throws aside the rule of scripture and acts on the pull of desire reaches neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the highest goal. Three things, all missed. And verse twenty-four, the chapter's last word: so let scripture be your measure in deciding what to do and what not to do. Know what the rule says, and act in this world. The word is shastra. It means teaching, a rule, a manual, sometimes a whole science. There are shastras for grammar, for architecture, for music, and for how to live. Here the contrast isn't scripture against thinking. It's scripture against kama, desire, the first of yesterday's three gates. The point is that desire makes a poor compass. It always points to itself. Hindus read this verse in more than one way. For some, the shastra is the Vedas and the texts that follow them, learned from a teacher. Others stress that the Gita itself is a shastra, and that knowing the rule means understanding its purpose, not just its letter. And notice what happens next. Chapter seventeen opens with Arjuna asking: what about people who don't follow the scripture's rules, but who worship with real faith? The Gita doesn't avoid the question. It takes it up in the very next verse. That's the word today: follow the scripture.
screen: `FREE OF THE THREE GATES.` · `DESIRE IS A POOR COMPASS.` · `LET SCRIPTURE BE YOUR MEASURE.` · `SHASTRA: TEACHING, RULE, MANUAL.` · then, large: `FOLLOW THE SCRIPTURE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of one decision on your mind right now. Notice what desire says about it: what do I want, right this minute? Let that voice finish. Then ask a second question: what would the best teaching I know say here? A line from a book, a grandparent's rule, something from these two hundred days. Hold both answers side by side, without choosing yet. Just see the difference. The bell holds the time.
Shastra, teaching, rule, authoritative text. Gita sixteen, twenty-four: let it be your measure for what to do and not do, rather than the pull of desire.
Your line: know the rule. Before one choice today, ask what you want, and then ask what the teaching says. Notice when they differ. Day two hundred fifteen.

216.title: Faith follows nature (17.1–17.6)
216.hook: the Gita says a person is made of their faith
216.tomorrow: Food, sacrifice, austerity, gift — three kinds each (17.7–17.22)
216.howItsDone: Shraddha, faith as trust and wholehearted commitment, is a key word in Hindu practice; Gita 17.3, 'a person is made of faith', is quoted by teachers to explain why sincere practice shapes a person.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shastra, follow the scripture, not desire. Let the teaching be your measure. Your line was know the rule. Did desire and the teaching disagree today? And Arjuna had a question waiting. Day two hundred sixteen.

A grandmother who never read the books. She couldn't recite a single verse in Sanskrit, but she lit the lamp every evening, for as long as anyone can remember, and never once missed it. She didn't know the rules. But she had something. Arjuna has just heard Krishna say, let scripture be your measure. His next question could be about people like her. Chapter seventeen opens with it. What about them, Krishna? The ones who set aside the rules, but worship with faith?
screen: `SHE NEVER READ THE BOOKS.` → `A LAMP LIT EVERY EVENING.` → `WHAT ABOUT HER FAITH?`

segments.voice: Verse one is Arjuna's question: those who set aside the rule of scripture but worship full of faith, what is their standing? Is it sattva, rajas or tamas? He's using the three threads from chapter fourteen. Krishna doesn't say, those people are wrong. He says, verse two: faith comes in three kinds, born of each person's own nature. Then verse three. Everyone's faith takes the shape of their inner being. A person is made of faith. Shraddhamayo 'yam purushah. Whatever their faith is, that's what they are. Yo yac-chraddhah sa eva sah. That's a strong claim. Not: a person has a faith. A person is made of it. What someone trusts, what they give themselves to, shapes who they become. The word is shraddha, often translated faith. Some teachers take it apart as shrat, truth or the heart, and dha, to place: placing your heart. So it's less about believing a list of statements, more about where you set your trust. Then the chapter begins to sort. Verse four: the clear-hearted worship the gods; the restless worship yakshas and rakshasas, spirits of wealth and power; the heavy worship ghosts. And verses five and six warn about people who torture their own bodies with harsh practices the scriptures never taught, full of show and ego. They hurt the body, Krishna says, and they hurt me, who lives inside it. So faith follows nature. That's the word today: faith follows nature.
screen: `WHAT ABOUT FAITH WITHOUT RULES?` · `FAITH COMES IN THREE KINDS.` · `A PERSON IS MADE OF FAITH.` · `NO SHOW, NO SELF-TORTURE.` · then, large: `FAITH FOLLOWS NATURE.`

segments.voice: Sit, and ask gently: where do I place my heart? Not what do I say I believe, but what do I actually trust, day to day? Let a few answers come. Maybe a person. A routine. Money. A practice. God. Your own effort. No answer is wrong. Just notice which ones rise first, and how each one feels in the body. The Gita says you are made of this. The bell holds the time.
Shraddha, faith, trust. Gita seventeen, three: each person's faith takes the shape of their nature; a person is made of it, and as their faith is, so are they.
Your line: as you believe. Today, notice one thing you trust without thinking about it. Ask if it's shaping you the way you'd want. Day two hundred sixteen.

original.note: Sanskrit: shraddha, faith, trust; some teachers explain it as placing (dha) the heart or truth (shrat).

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing things without proof.
what it means: in Gita 17, faith is where you place your heart, and you become what you place it in.
what a scholar hears: 17.3 'shraddhamayo 'yam purusho yo yac-chraddhah sa eva sah'; shraddha is sometimes analyzed as shrat + dha, though the etymology is debated.

217.title: Food, sacrifice, austerity, gift — three kinds each (17.7–17.22)
217.hook: the Gita sorts your lunch, your worship, your discipline and your giving into three kinds
217.howItsDone: Some Hindus think about food in terms of the three gunas, preferring fresh, simple, sattvic food, especially before worship; Gita 17.20's gift given without hope of return is cited in teaching on dana, charity.

segments.voice: Yesterday: shraddha, faith follows nature. A person is made of faith. Your line was as you believe. Did you notice something you trust without thinking? Today, the three threads come to the kitchen table. Day two hundred seventeen.

Open the fridge at midnight. There's the leftover takeout from three days ago. There's the extra-spicy chips that'll burn all the way down. And there's a bowl of warm rice and dal someone made with care. A hand hovers. A holy book might seem to have nothing to say here. The Gita does. After saying that faith comes in three kinds, chapter seventeen applies the three threads to four ordinary things: what you eat, how you worship, how you discipline yourself, and how you give.
screen: `THE FRIDGE AT MIDNIGHT.` → `LEFTOVERS, CHIPS, OR WARM DAL?` → `THE GITA HAS AN OPINION.`

segments.voice: Start with food. Verse eight: sattvic food lengthens life and brings purity, strength, health, happiness and cheer. It's tasty, smooth, nourishing and pleasant. Verse nine: rajasic food is bitter, sour, salty, very hot, pungent, dry and burning. It brings pain, grief and sickness. Verse ten: tamasic food is stale, flavorless, spoiled, leftover, impure. Some commentators read that 'very' as reaching across the whole list, so the trouble is excess, not flavor. Then sacrifice, the offering. Sattvic: done because it ought to be done, not for a reward. Rajasic: done for the reward, or for show. Tamasic: done carelessly, without faith, without the proper words, without sharing food with others. Then austerity, tapas, discipline, in three places. Of the body: honoring teachers, cleanliness, straightness, doing no harm. Of speech, verse fifteen: words that don't upset people, that are true, kind and helpful. Of the mind: calm, gentleness, silence, self-control. Done with faith and no wish for reward, it's sattvic. Done for honor and praise, rajasic. Done to torture yourself or harm someone else, tamasic. And last, the gift. Verse twenty: a gift given simply because it should be given, to someone who can't pay you back, at the right time and place, to the right person, that gift is sattvic. Given to get something back, or grudgingly: rajasic. Given with contempt, at the wrong time, to the wrong person: tamasic. Four ordinary things, three kinds each. So the week closes: tejas, the light in the sun, the one beyond, the divine and the demonic, the scripture, faith, and now food. That's the word today: food.
screen: `FOOD: NOURISHING, TOO MUCH, STALE.` · `SACRIFICE: DUTY, SHOW, CARELESS.` · `AUSTERITY OF BODY, SPEECH, MIND.` · `THE GIFT THAT WANTS NOTHING BACK.` · then, large: `FOOD.`

segments.voice: Sit, and think of your last meal. How did it leave you? Light and clear? Buzzing or burning? Heavy and dull? No judgment, just notice. Then think of the last thing you gave someone: time, money, a favor. Was there a hope of getting something back? Now think of one small gift you could give today to someone who can't repay you. Hold it in mind. The bell holds the time.
Food. Gita seventeen: food, sacrifice, austerity and gift each come in three kinds, sattvic, rajasic and tamasic, and the kind shapes the one who eats, offers or gives.
Your line: which kind. At your next meal, and your next gift, ask quietly: which kind is this? Then choose. Day two hundred seventeen.

original.note: Sanskrit: sattvika, of the nature of sattva: clear, nourishing, balanced. the same pattern gives rajasika and tamasika.

trapdoor: what you thought: this chapter is a diet plan.
